sections.overview: Nuttalliella namaqua is the only living species in its tick family, Nuttalliellidae. It is rarely collected, so basic parts of its biology remain poorly known.
sections.identification: Its leathery, folded cuticle and partly hardened dorsal shield combine traits associated with soft and hard ticks. “Living fossil” is informal shorthand, not a literal fossil or a direct ancestor of other ticks.
sections.habitat: Records come from southern and eastern Africa, including South Africa, Namibia, Tanzania, Botswana and Mozambique. Specimens have been found beneath stones, in rock crevices, on open ground and in bird nests.
sections.diet: Like other ticks, it feeds on vertebrate blood. Records from rodents, reptiles and other animals suggest several possible hosts, but its host preferences are not settled.
sections.behavior: The tick is elusive and appears to feed rapidly, which helps explain why few specimens have been collected while attached to a host. Its life cycle in the wild is still unresolved.
sections.reproduction: Males and immature stages have been described, and females kept in laboratory conditions laid eggs that hatched. These observations confirm reproduction, but not a complete natural life cycle.
sections.ecology: Anatomical and molecular studies place this unusual lineage near the base of the tick tree, apart from both hard-tick and soft-tick families.
sections.conservation: The species has no assessed IUCN Red List category. Its rarity in collections is not evidence that its population is declining.
